claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers is primarily governed by the accumulation and interaction of misfit-induced dislocation arrays at nanoscale interfaces.
Chemically sharper interfaces amplify local lattice distortion.
Thinner constituent layers amplify local lattice distortion.
Sharper interfaces and thinner layers amplify short-range-order effects.
Lattice misfit plays a significant role in creep behavior.
Enhanced lattice distortion and short-range order increase stress concentrations at FCC/BCC interfaces.
Interfacial stress concentrations trigger dislocation nucleation at chemically sharp interfaces during sustained loading.
Interfacial stress concentrations sustain dislocation motion across the multilayer.
Thinner layers and chemically abrupt interfaces produce a higher density of misfit dislocations.
Accumulation and interaction of misfit dislocations facilitate creep by initiating localized deformation events.
The multilayer architecture governs the balance between strength and deformation tolerance.
Relative to the baseline, thinner layers and sharper interfaces will increase the density of interfacial misfit-dislocation arrays.
Relative to the baseline, thinner layers and sharper interfaces will accelerate the creep strain rate.
Thicker layers or more compositionally graded interfaces will reduce creep rate by diminishing localized interfacial stress concentrations.
Creep mechanisms can change with temperature and applied stress, including regimes involving grain-boundary diffusion, lattice diffusion, and dislocations.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the nanoscale multilayer remains intact without layer coarsening or additional interdiffusion.
The proposed mechanism applies in a dislocation-mediated creep regime without phase transformations or dominant extraneous diffusion mechanisms.
